# Compact Object Headers in a Spring Boot Container

A container memory limit caps the memory available to a Java process, but it
does not show how much application data fits in the heap. On supported 64-bit
HotSpot builds, Java 25 can reduce object headers from 96 or 128 bits to 64 bits
with `-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders`. The effect depends on the number and layout
of objects the application creates.

This example uses the workshop’s Spring Boot quotes application. Flyway loads
200 quotes into an H2 in-memory database. Every `/quote/random` request loads
the whole quote catalogue as Java objects before returning one quote. We run the
same JAR and image in two containers, then compare post-GC live heap and
behaviour under 1,000 requests with compact headers off and on.

Reading the whole table to choose one quote is deliberately inefficient. It
creates a repeatable allocation workload for this exercise, not a recommended
query pattern. With this small catalogue, any memory saving may be modest. This
focused example does not cover every aspect of running Java
in containers. See [all-in-one-spring-boot](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md)
for the more holistic example.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- run identical Java 25 containers with compact headers off and on;
- compare post-GC live-object bytes and observe both JVMs under the same request
  load; and
- distinguish a heap-footprint result from throughput or container RSS.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) with a running daemon

- `curl`, `jq`, `tree`, and `hey`

## The artefacts to inspect

Flyway creates the `quote` table in `V1__create_database.sql` and populates it
with 200 rows. The data is part of the application JAR. There is no startup
duplication component or external database. The integration test checks both the
row count and that JPA can materialise the catalogue.

```sql
CREATE TABLE quote
(
    id     INT AUTO_INCREMENT NOT NULL,
    author VARCHAR(32)  NOT NULL,
    quote  VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (id)
);
```

`QuoteService.random()` materialises every row as a `Quote` with an identifier,
author, and quote text. It copies the results into an `ArrayList`, shuffles
them, and returns one. Each request therefore allocates many short-lived
objects. H2 also retains the catalogue in the heap between requests.

```java
package demo.quote;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

import static java.util.Objects.requireNonNull;

@Service
public class QuoteService {

    private final QuoteRepository repository;

    public QuoteService(final QuoteRepository repository) {
        this.repository = requireNonNull(repository, "The quote repository cannot be null");
    }

    public Optional<Quote> random() {
        /* Returns a random quote, inefficiently, by loading all the quotes from
            the database and then picking one at random. A more efficient way
            would have fetched the count of quotes in the table and then return
            the one found at a random index using the SQL LIMIT and OFFSET. */
        final List<Quote> quotes = new ArrayList<>(repository.findAll());

        if (quotes.isEmpty()) {
            return Optional.empty();
        }

        Collections.shuffle(quotes);
        return Optional.of(quotes.getFirst());
    }
}
```

The Dockerfile copies the same packaged JAR into a full JDK image for both runs.
The full JDK provides `jcmd` for the heap inspection. JVM options are supplied
at launch, so the image itself does not change.

```dockerfile
FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
WORKDIR "/opt/app"

ARG JAR_FILE="./target/compact-object-headers-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar"
COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

## Build the application

Build the application JAR once, then use it to create one image for both runs.
This keeps the application and image constant while comparing the two
object-header settings.

1. Build and test the application.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   Optionally, confirm that the packaged JAR exists.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target'
   ```

   The packaged application JAR.

   ```
   ./target
   ├── compact-object-headers-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── compact-object-headers-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. Build one image from the packaged JAR.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
     --tag 'demo:compact-object-headers-spring-boot' \
     '.'
   ```

   Both runs use this image. Set `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS` when starting each container
   to disable or enable compact object headers.

## Guided walkthrough

Run the same image twice: first with compact object headers disabled, then with
them enabled. Give both containers the same memory limit and heap settings, with
enough headroom for this workload. The object-header option is the only JVM
setting to change. Check the GC results to see whether full collections
occurred; a generous memory limit does not rule them out.

### Baseline (compact headers explicitly disabled)

Run the application with compact object headers disabled to establish a
baseline. We will compare its live-object size, request performance, and GC
activity with a second run using compact headers.

1. Start the baseline with compact object headers disabled.

   The container has a 512 MiB memory limit; HotSpot is configured to use up to
   75% of available memory for the heap.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --detach \
     --rm \
     --name 'demo-coh-standard' \
     --memory '512m' \
     --publish '8080:8080' \
     --env 'JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS=-XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders -XX:MinRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0' \
     'demo:compact-object-headers-spring-boot'
   ```

   Wait until the application can serve requests. Startup includes loading the
   quote catalogue into H2.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   The container should start and become available in a couple of seconds.

2. Request a quote to confirm that the endpoint responds.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "J. R. R. Tolkien",
     "id": 94,
     "quote": "I will not say: do not weep; for not all tears are an evil."
   }
   ```

3. Check that HotSpot reports `UseCompactObjectHeaders` as false.

   ```shell
   docker exec 'demo-coh-standard' jcmd 1 VM.flags -all | grep 'UseCompactObjectHeaders'
   ```

   The reported value must be false for the baseline.

   ```
        bool UseCompactObjectHeaders                  = false                          {product lp64_product} {command line}
   ```

4. Record the live-object total before the request load.

   ```shell
   docker exec 'demo-coh-standard' jcmd 1 GC.class_histogram \
     | awk '/^Total/ { print "standard live bytes: " $3 }'
   ```

   The live-object totals for the baseline.

   ```
   standard live bytes: 23849048
   ```

   `GC.class_histogram` normally triggers a full GC, then reports live objects
   and their shallow sizes. The third column of the `Total` line gives the total
   bytes. Record this value for comparison with the compact-header run; it is
   not a measure of container memory usage.

5. Run the stress test

   Record the cumulative young-generation and full GC counts before sending
   requests. We will compare them with the counts afterwards to find how many
   collections occurred during the load test. The earlier class histogram may
   already have triggered a full GC, so these starting counts need not be zero.

   ```shell
   docker exec demo-coh-standard jstat -gcutil 1 |
     awk 'NR == 1 { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) column[$i] = i; next }
         NR == 2 { printf "YGC=%s FGC=%s\n", $(column["YGC"]), $(column["FGC"]) }'
   ```

   Cumulative young-generation and full GC counts before the load test.

   ```
   YGC=126 FGC=4
   ```

   Send 10,000 requests with 8 concurrent workers, then record the counts
   again. `hey` allows up to 60 seconds for each request.

   ```shell
   hey -n=10000 -c=8 -t=60 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random'
   ```

   The stress test results

   ```
   Summary:
     Total:	2.2843 secs
     Slowest:	0.0220 secs
     Fastest:	0.0005 secs
     Average:	0.0018 secs
     Requests/sec:	4377.6378


   Response time histogram:
     0.001 [1]	|
     0.003 [8400]	|■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■
     0.005 [1405]	|■■■■■■■
     0.007 [151]	|■
     0.009 [21]	|
     0.011 [8]	|
     0.013 [6]	|
     0.016 [2]	|
     0.018 [3]	|
     0.020 [2]	|
     0.022 [1]	|


   Latency distribution:
     10%% in 0.0009 secs
     25%% in 0.0011 secs
     50%% in 0.0015 secs
     75%% in 0.0023 secs
     90%% in 0.0031 secs
     95%% in 0.0038 secs
     99%% in 0.0056 secs

   Details (average, fastest, slowest):
     DNS+dialup:	0.0000 secs, 0.0000 secs, 0.0026 secs
     DNS-lookup:	0.0000 secs, 0.0000 secs, 0.0014 secs
     req write:	0.0000 secs, 0.0000 secs, 0.0010 secs
     resp wait:	0.0017 secs, 0.0005 secs, 0.0191 secs
     resp read:	0.0001 secs, 0.0000 secs, 0.0029 secs

   Status code distribution:
     [200]	10000 responses
   ```

   Record the cumulative GC counts again after the load test. Subtract the
   counts recorded before the test to see how many young-generation and full
   collections occurred while the requests were running.

   ```shell
   docker exec demo-coh-standard jstat -gcutil 1 |
     awk 'NR == 1 { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) column[$i] = i; next }
         NR == 2 { printf "YGC=%s FGC=%s\n", $(column["YGC"]), $(column["FGC"]) }'
   ```

   Cumulative young-generation and full GC counts after the load test.

   ```
   YGC=191 FGC=4
   ```

   Compare the request rate and 95th percentile latency with the second run.
   Calculate GC events during this load by subtracting the counts recorded
   before it from those recorded afterwards. These are observations from this
   machine and workload, not portable performance results.

   | Runtime            | No Compact Object Headers |
   | ------------------ | ------------------------: |
   | Live-object totals |        `23849048` (bytes) |
   | Throughput         |     `4377.6378` (req/sec) |
   | Latency (P95)      |            `0.0038` (sec) |
   | Young GC Count     |                      `65` |
   | Full GC Count      |                       `0` |

   Treat these numbers as local observations from this machine and run, not as
   portable benchmarks. This is the baseline for the comparisons that follow.

6. Stop the baseline container so the second run can use the same host
   port.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'demo-coh-standard'
   ```

### Compact object headers enabled

Run the same application image with compact object headers enabled. Use the same
memory limit, heap settings, and request load as the baseline so the
object-header option is the JVM setting being compared.

1. Start the container with compact object headers enabled.

   As in the baseline run, the container has a 512 MiB memory limit and HotSpot is
   configured to use up to 75% of available memory for the heap.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --detach \
     --rm \
     --name 'demo-coh-compact' \
     --memory '512m' \
     --publish '8080:8080' \
     --env 'JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS=-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders -XX:MinRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0' \
     'demo:compact-object-headers-spring-boot'
   ```

   Wait until the application can serve requests. Startup includes loading the
   quote catalogue into H2.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   The container should start and become available in a couple of seconds.

2. Request a quote to confirm that the endpoint responds.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Friedrich Nietzsche",
     "id": 64,
     "quote": "That which does not kill us makes us stronger."
   }
   ```

3. Check that HotSpot reports `UseCompactObjectHeaders` as true.

   ```shell
   docker exec 'demo-coh-compact' jcmd 1 VM.flags -all | grep 'UseCompactObjectHeaders'
   ```

   HotSpot reports that compact object headers are enabled.

   ```
        bool UseCompactObjectHeaders                  = true                           {product lp64_product} {command line}
   ```

4. Record the live-object total before the request load.

   ```shell
   docker exec 'demo-coh-compact' jcmd 1 GC.class_histogram \
     | awk '/^Total/ { print "compact live bytes: " $3 }'
   ```

   Live-object bytes with compact object headers enabled.

   ```
   compact live bytes: 21548672
   ```

   `GC.class_histogram` normally triggers a full GC, then reports live objects
   and their shallow sizes. Compare the total bytes with the baseline
   measurement taken at the same point in the walkthrough. This value does not
   measure container memory usage.

5. Run the same stress test as the baseline.

   Record the cumulative young-generation and full GC counts before sending
   requests. The histogram may already have triggered a full GC, so the starting
   full GC count need not be zero.

   ```shell
   docker exec demo-coh-compact jstat -gcutil 1 |
     awk 'NR == 1 { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) column[$i] = i; next }
         NR == 2 { printf "YGC=%s FGC=%s\n", $(column["YGC"]), $(column["FGC"]) }'
   ```

   Cumulative young-generation and full GC counts before the load test.

   ```
   YGC=126 FGC=4
   ```

   Send 10,000 requests with 8 concurrent workers. `hey` allows up to 60
   seconds for each request.

   ```shell
   hey -n=10000 -c=8 -t=60 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random'
   ```

   The stress test results

   Record the cumulative GC counts again. Subtract the starting counts to find
   how many collections occurred during this load test.

   ```shell
   docker exec demo-coh-compact jstat -gcutil 1 |
     awk 'NR == 1 { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) column[$i] = i; next }
         NR == 2 { printf "YGC=%s FGC=%s\n", $(column["YGC"]), $(column["FGC"]) }'
   ```

   Cumulative young-generation and full GC counts after the load test.

   ```
   YGC=192 FGC=4
   ```

   Compare the measurements from both runs. The live-object totals show retained
   shallow object bytes after a diagnostic full GC. The request rate, 95th
   percentile latency, and GC counts describe what happened during each load
   test; they do not establish a portable performance gain.

   | Runtime            | No Compact Object Headers | Compact Object Headers |
   | ------------------ | ------------------------: | ---------------------: |
   | Live-object totals |        `23849048` (bytes) |     `21548672` (bytes) |

   | Latency (P95)      |            `0.0038` (sec) |         `0.0038` (sec) |
   | Young GC Count     |                      `65` |                   `66` |
   | Full GC Count      |                       `0` |                    `0` |

6. Stop the compact-header container.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'demo-coh-compact'
   ```

- [JEP 519: Compact Object Headers](https://openjdk.org/jeps/519)
- [Oracle JDK 25 GC Tuning Guide: Compact Object Headers](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/gctuning/other-considerations.html)

## Key takeaways and trade-offs

- Flyway supplies a fixed 200-quote catalogue; the same application and image
  run under both Java 25 header layouts.
- Compact headers can reduce the live Java heap for an object-heavy application.
  Measure the effect on the actual workload.
- Repeated full-table reads create allocation pressure, but throughput, GC
  activity, and container RSS need separate interpretation. The full-table read
  and full-GC diagnostic are workshop choices.
